title: Remembering 'Poltergeist' Star Dominique Dunne on Her Birthday
excerpt: Dominique Dunne, who played Dana in Poltergeist, would have turned 67 today. Her life, her career and the 1983 trial of the man who killed her at 22.
content:
Dominique Dunne, who played Dana Freeling in Poltergeist, was born on November 23, 1959, and would have turned 67 today. She made one feature film before she was killed at 22, and the judge at her killer’s trial later wrote that the man “got away with murder.”

She Grew Up in a Family of Writers and Actors

Dunne was born in Santa Monica, California, the youngest child of writer and producer Dominick Dunne and Ellen Griffin Dunne. Her brother Griffin Dunne is an actor, and her uncle and aunt were the writers John Gregory Dunne and Joan Didion.

‘Poltergeist’ Was Her Only Feature Film

She began in television, with roles that included the TV movie The Day the Loving Stopped and the Western The Shadow Riders. Poltergeist followed in June 1982, with Dunne as the teenage daughter of the Freeling family, and it was the only theatrical film she appeared in. Her death five months after it opened is one of the events behind the legend of the Poltergeist curse.

That fall she filmed an episode of Hill Street Blues and began rehearsing for the miniseries V.

She Was Killed by Her Ex-Boyfriend in 1982

Dunne met John Thomas Sweeney, a sous-chef at the Los Angeles restaurant Ma Maison, at a party in 1981, and the two moved into a house in West Hollywood. On September 26, 1982, Sweeney grabbed her by the throat during an argument. She ended the relationship and had the locks changed. The next day she filmed her Hill Street Blues episode, and her father later wrote in Vanity Fair that the marks on her neck in it were real.

On the night of October 30, 1982, Dunne was at home rehearsing for V with actor David Packer when Sweeney came to the house. She agreed to speak with him on the porch, and he strangled her beside the driveway. She never regained consciousness and died at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center on November 4, 1982, after her parents consented to removing life support. Her heart and kidneys were donated at her mother’s request.

The Judge Kept Sweeney’s History of Violence From the Jury

Sweeney was charged with first-degree murder, and his trial began in August 1983 before Judge Burton S. Katz. Katz ruled that a former girlfriend of Sweeney’s, Lillian Pierce, could not tell the jury about the times she said he had assaulted her, and he excluded testimony from Dunne’s mother and friends about how Sweeney had treated her. Katz also dropped the first-degree murder charge, which left the jury to choose between second-degree murder and manslaughter.

On September 21, 1983, after eight days of deliberation, the jury acquitted Sweeney of second-degree murder and convicted him of voluntary manslaughter, along with a misdemeanor assault for the September attack. The jury foreman later said the jurors would have convicted Sweeney of murder had they heard all of the evidence. Katz sentenced him to six and a half years, and Sweeney was released in 1986.

Her Parents Became Advocates for Victims

Dominick Dunne kept a journal during the trial, and it was published in the March 1984 issue of Vanity Fair as “Justice: A Father’s Account of the Trial of his Daughter’s Killer.” About a year after her daughter’s death, Ellen Griffin Dunne founded Justice for Homicide Victims, a victims’ rights group. Dominique Dunne is buried at Westwood Village Memorial Park in Los Angeles.
